decks.title: Body Fluids and Circulation — Part 1: blood, blood groups and lymph
goals: State the functions of plasma proteins and of each type of blood corpuscle, and outline blood clotting
Predict compatible donors and recipients in the ABO and Rh systems and explain erythroblastosis foetalis
Compare lymph with blood and open with closed circulation

slides.heading: Body Fluids and Circulation
slides.body_md: Part 1: blood, blood groups, lymph and the types of circulatory system.

visual.alt: Flow of the topics of part one

slides.narration: Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, wastes and hormones round the body, and helps to defend it. In this part we look at what blood is made of, how it clots, how blood groups decide who can donate to whom, and how lymph and different circulatory systems compare.

slides.heading: Plasma and plasma proteins
slides.body_md: **Blood** is a fluid connective tissue: about **55 percent plasma** and **45 percent formed elements**. Plasma is **90 to 92 percent water** and **6 to 8 percent proteins**, with small amounts of salts, glucose, amino acids, fats, hormones and wastes.

rows: Maintains the osmotic balance between blood and tissues
Blood clotting; plasma without it is serum

visual.alt: Table of plasma proteins and their functions

slides.narration: Plasma is the liquid part of blood. Most of it is water, and the rest includes three groups of proteins. Albumin holds water in the blood, globulins include antibodies, and fibrinogen is needed for clotting. Serum is plasma that has lost its clotting factors.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: one bag of donated blood
slides.body_md: A blood bank collects **450 mL** of blood in one bag. Estimate the volume of plasma and cells, and of water and protein in the plasma.
bullets: Plasma $= 55/100 \times 450 = 247.5$ mL; formed elements $= 450 - 247.5 = 202.5$ mL.
Water (about 92 percent of the plasma) $= 92/100 \times 247.5 = 227.7$ mL.
Proteins (about 7 percent) $= 7/100 \times 247.5 \approx 17.33$ mL.

visual.alt: Worked table of the volumes in one bag of blood

slides.narration: Take fifty five percent of the bag for plasma, and the rest is cells. Then take about ninety two percent of the plasma for water and about seven percent for protein. The shares are approximate, since books give slightly different ranges.

slides.heading: Red blood cells and platelets
slides.body_md: The **formed elements** are the erythrocytes, leucocytes and platelets.

rows: Biconcave, no nucleus, contain haemoglobin; made in red bone marrow; life about 120 days; destroyed in the spleen
Cell fragments of megakaryocytes of the bone marrow

visual.alt: Table of red blood cells and platelets

slides.narration: Mature red cells of mammals have no nucleus, which leaves more room for haemoglobin. They live about four months and are broken down in the spleen. Platelets are not whole cells but fragments, and they release the substances that start clotting.

slides.heading: White blood cells
slides.body_md: **Leucocytes** are colourless, nucleated cells, **6000 to 8000 per mm³**, that defend the body. They are **granulocytes** (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) or **agranulocytes** (lymphocytes, monocytes).

rows: B cells make antibodies; T cells give cell-mediated immunity
Release histamine, heparin and serotonin in inflammation

visual.alt: Table of the five types of white blood cell

slides.narration: Neutrophils are the commonest white cells and swallow bacteria. Lymphocytes are the key cells of immunity. Monocytes become macrophages, eosinophils deal with allergy and parasites, and basophils release chemicals that are involved in inflammation.

slides.heading: Quick check: red cells
slides.body_md: Link a feature of the mammalian red cell with its job.
slides.narration: Quick check. Why does a mature red cell have no nucleus?

slides.heading: Coagulation of blood
slides.body_md: At an injury, **platelets and damaged tissue** release **thromboplastin** (clotting factors). With **Ca²⁺**, it converts **prothrombin** (inactive) into **thrombin**. Thrombin converts soluble **fibrinogen** into insoluble **fibrin** threads, which trap blood cells to form the **clot**.

nodes.label: Injury: platelets and tissue release thromboplastin
Fibrin mesh traps blood cells: clot

visual.alt: Flow of the cascade of blood clotting

slides.narration: Clotting is a chain of steps. Injury releases thromboplastin, which with calcium ions turns prothrombin into thrombin. Thrombin changes fibrinogen into fibrin threads. The threads form a mesh that traps red cells and seals the wound.

slides.heading: Quick check: clotting
slides.body_md: Predict the result of an experiment on the clotting cascade.
slides.narration: Quick check. What does thrombin act on?

slides.heading: ABO blood groups (Landsteiner)
slides.body_md: **Karl Landsteiner** discovered the ABO groups in 1900. The group depends on the **antigens** on the red cells, and the plasma holds **antibodies** against the antigens a person lacks.

visual.alt: Table of ABO groups with antigens, antibodies and compatible donors and recipients

slides.narration: A person makes antibodies against the antigens that the red cells lack. If the wrong blood is given, these antibodies make the donor cells clump together. Group O red cells have no antigens, so they can go to anyone, while group AB people have no antibodies and can receive from anyone.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: who can give to whom
slides.body_md: Red cells can be given safely if the donor has **no antigen (A, B or Rh) that the recipient lacks**. Using all eight types:
bullets: A negative donor can give to 4 types: A negative, A positive, AB negative, AB positive.
A B negative patient can receive from 2 types: O negative and B negative.
O negative can give to all 8 types; AB positive can receive from all 8.

visual.alt: Worked table of numbers of compatible recipients and donors

slides.narration: Check three things: antigen A, antigen B and the Rh antigen. If the donor has one that the recipient lacks, the recipient will react. This is why group O negative is the universal donor and group AB positive is the universal recipient.

slides.heading: Quick check: donors
slides.body_md: Choose the safe donors for a patient.
slides.narration: Quick check. Check the antigens of each donor against the patient.

slides.heading: Rh factor and erythroblastosis foetalis
slides.body_md: The **Rh antigen** was found by **Landsteiner and Wiener** in the rhesus monkey; about **80 to 85 percent** of people are **Rh positive**. If an **Rh-negative mother** carries an **Rh-positive foetus**, her blood may be sensitised; she is then given **anti-Rh antibodies** soon after the first delivery to prevent harm to later babies.

nodes.label: At delivery foetal red cells reach the mother
Second Rh-positive baby: antibodies cross the placenta and destroy its red cells

visual.alt: Flow of how erythroblastosis foetalis arises

slides.narration: The first baby is usually safe, because the mother makes few antibodies during that pregnancy. At delivery some of the baby’s red cells enter her blood and she makes anti-Rh antibodies. In a later pregnancy these cross the placenta and destroy the red cells of an Rh-positive foetus, causing erythroblastosis foetalis.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: blood groups of children
slides.body_md: A father of group AB marries a mother of group A who has an O allele (genotype IᴬIᴮ × Iᴬi). The father is Rh positive (Dd) and the mother Rh negative (dd). Predict the children.
bullets: ABO: gametes $I^A, I^B$ and $I^A, i$ give $I^A I^A$, $I^A i$ (group A: 0.5), $I^A I^B$ (AB: 0.25) and $I^B i$ (B: 0.25).
Rh: $Dd \times dd$ gives Rh positive with probability 0.5.
No child can be group O.

visual.alt: Worked table of ABO probabilities of the children

slides.narration: Write the gametes of each parent and combine them. Half the children are group A, a quarter are AB and a quarter are B. The father has no O allele, so group O cannot occur. For the Rh factor, half the children are Rh positive, which is a risk for an Rh-negative mother.

slides.heading: Quick check: Rh incompatibility
slides.body_md: Decide when an Rh-negative mother needs treatment.
slides.narration: Quick check. In which pregnancy is the foetus at risk?

slides.heading: Lymph and the lymphatic system
slides.body_md: Some fluid leaves the capillaries as **tissue fluid**. Most returns to the blood; the rest enters the **lymph capillaries** and flows through lymph vessels and **lymph nodes** back to veins near the heart.

visual.alt: Table comparing blood and lymph

slides.narration: Lymph is like plasma without red cells and with fewer proteins. Lymph nodes filter the lymph, trap germs, and house lymphocytes and phagocytes. Lymph also returns fluid and proteins to the blood and carries absorbed fats from the intestine.

slides.heading: Open and closed circulatory systems
slides.body_md: In an **open** system the heart pumps blood into **open spaces (sinuses)**; in a **closed** system blood stays in **vessels**.

visual.alt: Table comparing open and closed circulatory systems

slides.narration: Arthropods and most molluscs have an open system, where blood bathes the tissues directly. Earthworms and all vertebrates have a closed system, in which blood stays inside vessels, so its flow can be controlled and directed more precisely.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Blood: 55 percent plasma, 45 percent formed elements; plasma proteins albumin, globulins and fibrinogen.
Corpuscles: RBC carry oxygen; WBC defend; platelets help clotting.
Clotting: thromboplastin, prothrombin to thrombin (Ca²⁺), fibrinogen to fibrin, clot.
ABO and Rh: Landsteiner; O universal donor, AB universal recipient; Rh incompatibility and erythroblastosis foetalis.
Lymph: less protein, no red cells; lymph nodes filter; open and closed circulation.

visual.alt: Summary table of part one

slides.narration: To recap: blood is plasma and cells, each with its job. Clotting seals wounds by turning fibrinogen into fibrin. Blood groups depend on antigens and antibodies, and Rh incompatibility can harm a second child. Lymph returns tissue fluid to the blood and helps defence.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the **antigen and the antibody** when explaining a transfusion reaction.
For Rh problems, state that the **first baby** is usually unharmed and the **second** is at risk.
Write the clotting steps in order, naming **Ca²⁺**.
Compare lymph with blood on **at least three points**.

rows: Group O has both anti-A and anti-B

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes and corrections

slides.narration: Exam tips. Name the antigen and the antibody in a transfusion answer. For Rh disease, remember it is the second child that is at risk. List the clotting steps in order. And give at least three differences between blood and lymph.

goals: Draw and label the internal structure of the heart and describe the cardiac cycle
Calculate cardiac output from heart rate and stroke volume
Label an ECG, describe the regulation of the heartbeat, and compare artery, vein and capillary
State the cause and effect of hypertension, coronary artery disease, angina and heart failure

slides.heading: The heart and the circulation
slides.body_md: Part 2: how the heart pumps, how its beat is controlled and measured, and how it can fail.

visual.alt: Flow of the topics of part two

slides.narration: The heart is a muscular double pump. In this part we study its chambers and valves, the stages of one heartbeat, the amount of blood it pumps, the way its beat starts and is recorded, the three kinds of blood vessel, and common disorders of circulation.

slides.heading: Internal structure of the human heart
slides.body_md: The heart lies in the **pericardium**, a double membrane. It has two **auricles** (atria) and two **ventricles**; the **left ventricle has the thickest wall**. **Valves** keep blood flowing one way: **tricuspid** (right), **bicuspid or mitral** (left), and **semilunar** valves at the aorta and pulmonary artery.

slides.narration: Blood from the body enters the right auricle through the vena cavae and passes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle. The ventricle pumps it to the lungs through the pulmonary artery. Blood from the lungs returns to the left auricle, passes the bicuspid valve to the left ventricle and leaves by the aorta.

slides.heading: Chambers, vessels and valves
slides.body_md: The right side carries **deoxygenated** blood and the left side **oxygenated** blood; the **septum** keeps them apart.

visual.alt: Table of the chambers of the heart with the vessels and valves

slides.narration: Each chamber has a fixed source, a fixed destination and a valve that stops backflow. Chordae tendineae hold the flaps of the atrioventricular valves so they do not turn inside out when the ventricles contract. The left ventricle is the thickest because it pumps blood round the whole body.

slides.heading: The cardiac cycle
slides.body_md: One heartbeat is a **cardiac cycle**: **atrial systole**, **ventricular systole** and **joint diastole**. With **75 beats a minute**, the cycle takes **0.8 second**: 0.1 + 0.3 + 0.4.

slides.narration: In atrial systole the auricles contract and finish filling the ventricles. In ventricular systole the ventricles contract, the valves between auricle and ventricle close, and the semilunar valves open to let blood out. In joint diastole all chambers relax and blood flows in from the veins.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the length of the cycle
slides.body_md: A man’s heart beats **80 times a minute**. Find the length of one cycle, and the joint diastole if atrial systole stays 0.1 s and ventricular systole 0.3 s.
bullets: Faster beating shortens **diastole** most; the heart gets less time to fill.

visual.alt: Worked table of cycle length and joint diastole at three heart rates

slides.narration: Divide sixty seconds by the number of beats. At eighty beats a minute one cycle lasts three quarters of a second. The contraction times stay about the same, so it is the resting phase that shrinks when the heart beats faster.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: cardiac output
slides.body_md: **Stroke volume** is the blood pumped by each ventricle in one beat; **cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate**. A woman’s heart rate is **64 per minute** and her stroke volume **85 mL**.
bullets: Cardiac output $= 85 \times 64 = 5440$ mL per minute $\approx 5.44$ L per minute.

visual.alt: Worked table of cardiac output

slides.narration: Multiply the blood pumped in one beat by the number of beats in a minute. A resting adult pumps about five litres a minute, and a trained athlete can pump the same amount with a slower heart, because each beat pushes out more blood.

slides.heading: Quick check: cardiac output
slides.body_md: Calculate a cardiac output from heart rate and stroke volume.
slides.narration: Quick check. Multiply the two numbers and check the units.

slides.heading: Regulation of the heartbeat
slides.body_md: The heart is **myogenic**: its beat starts in the **sino-atrial (SA) node**, the **pacemaker**. The impulse spreads to the **atrio-ventricular (AV) node**, then down the **bundle of His** and **Purkinje fibres** to the ventricles. The **autonomic nervous system** adjusts it: **sympathetic** nerves and **adrenaline** speed it up, **parasympathetic** (vagus) nerves slow it.

visual.alt: Flow of the conduction of the impulse through the nodal tissue

The distance between two **R peaks** is one cardiac cycle.

slides.narration: An artery has a thick, elastic wall and a narrow lumen because blood leaves the heart at high pressure. A vein has a thinner wall, a wide lumen and valves, because blood returns at low pressure. A capillary wall is one cell thick, which allows exchange with the tissues.

slides.heading: Double circulation
slides.body_md: Blood passes through the heart **twice** in each complete circuit: the **pulmonary circuit** (right side, to the lungs) and the **systemic circuit** (left side, to the body).

visual.alt: Flow of double circulation from the right ventricle to the lungs, the left side, the body and back

slides.narration: The right side sends deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and oxygenated blood returns to the left side. The left side then pumps it to the body. Because the two kinds of blood never mix, the tissues receive fully oxygenated blood at high pressure.

slides.heading: Blood pressure
slides.body_md: Blood pressure is measured with a **sphygmomanometer**. The **systolic** pressure is recorded while the ventricles contract, and the **diastolic** pressure while they relax.

rows: Pulse pressure (for 120 over 80 it is 40 mm Hg)

visual.alt: Table of blood pressure readings and their meaning

slides.narration: Normal blood pressure is about one hundred twenty over eighty millimetres of mercury. A reading of one hundred forty over ninety or more, found again and again, means hypertension. The first number is the systolic pressure and the second the diastolic.

slides.heading: Disorders of circulation
slides.body_md: Several disorders affect the heart and vessels.

rows: Strains the heart; harms brain, kidneys and heart
Deposits of calcium, fat and cholesterol narrow the arteries supplying the heart (atherosclerosis)
Insufficient oxygen to the heart muscle
Acute chest pain, often on effort
The heart cannot pump blood enough for the body

visual.alt: Table of disorders of circulation with causes and effects

slides.narration: High blood pressure forces the heart to work harder. In coronary artery disease the vessels that feed the heart narrow, which may cause angina, a pain that comes when the heart muscle lacks oxygen. In heart failure the heart cannot pump enough blood, and the lungs may become congested.

The ECG records the electrical events, and disorders arise from high pressure, narrowed coronary arteries or failure of the pump.

notes.title: Body Fluids and Circulation — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Blood: plasma, plasma proteins, blood corpuscles and coagulation
sections.body_md:
**Blood** is a fluid connective tissue made of **plasma** (about 55 percent) and **formed elements** (about 45 percent). **Plasma** is a straw-coloured fluid with **90 to 92 percent water** and **6 to 8 percent proteins**, and small amounts of salts, glucose, amino acids, lipids, hormones and wastes. A bag of 450 mL of blood therefore holds about 247.5 mL of plasma and 202.5 mL of cells.

**Plasma proteins:** **albumin** (maintains the osmotic balance between blood and tissues), **globulins** (defence; they include the antibodies) and **fibrinogen** (blood clotting); **prothrombin** and other clotting factors are also present. **Serum** is plasma from which the clotting factors (fibrinogen) have been removed.

**Blood corpuscles.**
- **Erythrocytes (RBC):** 5 to 5.5 million per mm³; biconcave, **no nucleus** in mammals, contain the red pigment **haemoglobin**; formed in the red bone marrow, life span about 120 days, destroyed in the spleen. **Function:** transport of oxygen (and some carbon dioxide).
- **Leucocytes (WBC):** 6000 to 8000 per mm³; nucleated and colourless. **Granulocytes:** **neutrophils** (60 to 65 percent; most abundant; phagocytic), **eosinophils** (2 to 3 percent; allergy and parasites), **basophils** (0.5 to 1 percent; release histamine, heparin and serotonin). **Agranulocytes:** **lymphocytes** (20 to 25 percent; B cells make antibodies, T cells give cell-mediated immunity) and **monocytes** (6 to 8 percent; become macrophages).
- **Platelets (thrombocytes):** 1.5 to 3.5 lakh per mm³; cell fragments of **megakaryocytes**; they help in **clotting**.

**Coagulation (brief).** At an injury, platelets and damaged tissue release **thromboplastin** (clotting factors). With **calcium ions**, thromboplastin converts the inactive **prothrombin** of plasma into the enzyme **thrombin**. Thrombin converts soluble **fibrinogen** into insoluble **fibrin** threads. The fibrin meshwork traps red cells, platelets and white cells to form a **clot** (the cascade). Anticoagulants such as **heparin** prevent clotting inside vessels; **citrate** binds calcium in stored blood. Vitamin K is needed by the liver to make prothrombin.

key_terms.definition_md: The straw-coloured liquid part of blood, about 55 percent of it.
Plasma without fibrinogen and the other clotting factors.
The enzyme that converts fibrinogen into fibrin.
Insoluble protein threads that form the framework of a clot.

sections.heading: 2. ABO blood groups and the Rh factor
sections.body_md:
**ABO groups (Landsteiner, 1900).** The ABO group depends on the presence of the **antigens A and B** on the surface of the red cells; the plasma contains **antibodies** against the antigens that are absent. **Group A:** antigen A, antibody anti-B. **Group B:** antigen B, antibody anti-A. **Group AB:** both antigens, no antibodies (**universal recipient**). **Group O:** no antigen, both anti-A and anti-B (**universal donor**). The group is inherited through three alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i. If blood of an unsuitable group is given, the antibodies of the recipient make the donor's red cells **agglutinate** (clump).

**Rh factor.** Another antigen, the **Rh antigen** (first seen in the **rhesus monkey**, by Landsteiner and Wiener), is present on the red cells of about **80 to 85 percent** of people (**Rh positive**); those who lack it are **Rh negative**. An Rh-negative person who receives Rh-positive blood makes anti-Rh antibodies, so Rh-negative patients must be given Rh-negative blood.

**Erythroblastosis foetalis.** If an **Rh-negative mother** carries an **Rh-positive foetus**, a little foetal blood can enter her blood at **delivery**. She makes **anti-Rh antibodies**. The **first baby** is usually safe, but in a **later pregnancy** with an Rh-positive foetus the antibodies cross the **placenta** and **destroy the red cells** of the foetus, causing anaemia, jaundice and sometimes death. The mother is given **anti-Rh antibodies** soon after the first delivery to prevent this.

**Compatibility.** Red cells can be given when the donor has no antigen (A, B or Rh) that the recipient lacks. Of the eight ABO-Rh types, O negative can donate to all eight and AB positive can receive from all eight.

key_terms.definition_md: A substance, here on the red cell surface, that can trigger the formation of antibodies.
The clumping of red cells when antibodies meet the matching antigen.
Group O (O negative for both systems): its red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigen.
Destruction of the red cells of an Rh-positive foetus by anti-Rh antibodies of an Rh-negative mother.

sections.heading: 3. Lymph, the lymphatic system and types of circulation
sections.body_md:
**Tissue fluid** leaks from the blood capillaries and bathes the cells. Most of it returns to the capillaries; the rest is collected by blind-ended **lymph capillaries** and flows as **lymph** through **lymph vessels** (with valves, so flow is one way) and **lymph nodes** into large veins near the heart. **Lymph** is a colourless fluid; compared with blood it has **no red cells**, **fewer proteins** and nutrients, and its white cells are mainly **lymphocytes**.

**Functions of lymph:** return of tissue fluid and proteins to the blood; absorption of digested **fats** through the **lacteals** of the villi; defence. **Lymph nodes** **filter** the lymph, trap and destroy germs with **phagocytes** and produce and store **lymphocytes**, which make antibodies.

**Open and closed circulation.** In an **open circulatory system** (arthropods such as cockroach, and most molluscs) the heart pumps blood into **open spaces (sinuses or haemocoel)** that bathe the tissues; pressure and speed are low. In a **closed circulatory system** (annelids such as the earthworm, and chordates) blood stays inside **vessels**, giving faster flow and better control.

key_terms.definition_md: A colourless fluid formed from tissue fluid; it flows in lymph vessels to the veins.
A small organ on lymph vessels that filters lymph and houses lymphocytes and phagocytes.

sections.heading: 4. The human heart, cardiac cycle, stroke volume and cardiac output
sections.body_md:
**External features.** The heart is a muscular organ of about the size of a closed fist, lying between the lungs, slightly tilted to the left, inside the **pericardium** (a double-layered membrane with fluid). **Internal structure.** It has four chambers: two thin-walled upper **auricles (atria)** and two thick-walled lower **ventricles**, separated by the **interatrial** and **interventricular septa**; the **left ventricle has the thickest wall**. The right auricle receives deoxygenated blood from the **superior and inferior vena cavae** and passes it through the **tricuspid valve** to the right ventricle, which pumps it through a **semilunar valve** into the **pulmonary artery**. The left auricle receives oxygenated blood from the **pulmonary veins** and passes it through the **bicuspid (mitral) valve** to the left ventricle, which pumps it through a semilunar valve into the **aorta**. The valves allow blood to flow in one direction only; **chordae tendineae** attached to papillary muscles prevent the flaps from turning inside out. (The valves' closing produces the two heart sounds, lub and dub.)

**Cardiac cycle.** The sequence of events in one heartbeat. At about 75 beats a minute a cycle lasts about 0.8 second: **atrial (auricular) systole** (0.1 s) pushes the last of the blood into the ventricles through open valves; **ventricular systole** (0.3 s) closes the valves between auricle and ventricle, opens the semilunar valves and sends blood into the aorta and the pulmonary artery; **joint diastole** (0.4 s) is the relaxation of all four chambers, during which the semilunar valves close and blood flows from the veins into the auricles and on to the ventricles.

**Stroke volume** is the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle in one beat (about 70 mL). **Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate**; in a healthy resting adult it is about 5 litres a minute. For a stroke volume of 85 mL and a rate of 64 a minute it is 5440 mL a minute. A trained athlete has a larger stroke volume and a slower resting rate.

sections.heading: 5. Regulation of the heartbeat, ECG, blood pressure, double circulation and blood vessels
sections.body_md:
**Regulation.** Human heart is **myogenic**: the beat arises in the heart muscle itself, in the **sino-atrial (SA) node** in the wall of the right auricle, the **pacemaker**. The impulse spreads over both auricles and reaches the **atrio-ventricular (AV) node**; it passes down the **atrio-ventricular bundle (bundle of His)**, its two branches and the **Purkinje fibres** into the ventricular walls. The **autonomic nervous system** can modify it through a **cardiac centre in the medulla**: **sympathetic** nerves increase the rate and the force of the beat, **parasympathetic** (vagus) nerves decrease them; the hormone **adrenaline** from the adrenal medulla increases the cardiac output.

**ECG.** An **electrocardiogram** is a record of the electrical activity of the heart. The **P wave** represents the electrical excitation (**depolarisation**) of the auricles, which leads to atrial contraction; the **QRS complex** represents depolarisation of the ventricles, which starts ventricular contraction; the **T wave** represents the return of the ventricles from the excited to the normal state (repolarisation). The distance between two R peaks gives one cycle, so the **heart rate** can be read from an ECG strip (for example, an R–R distance of 20 mm on paper at 25 mm per second is 0.8 second, or 75 beats a minute).

**Blood pressure.** Measured with a **sphygmomanometer**. **Systolic** pressure is recorded when the ventricles contract, **diastolic** pressure when they relax; the normal is about **120/80 mm Hg**, and repeated readings of **140/90 mm Hg or above** indicate **hypertension**.

**Double circulation.** Blood passes through the heart twice in each complete circuit: in the **pulmonary circulation** the right ventricle sends deoxygenated blood to the lungs and oxygenated blood returns to the left auricle; in the **systemic circulation** the left ventricle sends oxygenated blood to the body and deoxygenated blood returns by the vena cavae to the right auricle. The two kinds of blood are kept apart.

**Blood vessels.** **Arteries** carry blood away from the heart; the wall has three coats (tunica externa, tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibres, tunica intima of endothelium) and is thick, with a narrow lumen and no valves. **Veins** carry blood to the heart; the wall is thinner, the lumen wide and **valves** prevent backflow. **Capillaries** have a wall of a **single layer of endothelial cells**, allowing exchange of materials.

sections.heading: 6. Disorders of circulation
sections.body_md:
- **Hypertension (high blood pressure):** blood pressure of **140/90 mm Hg or above** on repeated readings. It makes the heart work harder and damages the heart, the brain and the kidneys.
- **Coronary artery disease (CAD):** also called atherosclerosis; **deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue** make the lumen of the arteries that supply the heart muscle narrow, so less blood and oxygen reach it.
- **Angina pectoris:** **acute chest pain** that appears when **not enough oxygen** reaches the heart muscle, often on effort; the pain can also be felt in the left arm. It can be a sign of coronary artery disease.
- **Heart failure:** the state when the heart is **not pumping blood effectively enough** to meet the needs of the body; it is sometimes called **congestive heart failure** because the **lungs** can get congested. It is **not** the same as cardiac arrest (the heart stops beating) or a heart attack (sudden damage to heart muscle).

Books use somewhat different wording, and the syllabus asks for the cause and effect of each disorder.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying that group O has no antibodies (it has both anti-A and anti-B), or that group AB has antibodies (it has none).
- Forgetting that the first Rh-positive baby is usually safe and that the risk is to the second.
- Writing the clotting steps out of order or leaving out calcium ions.
- Placing the bicuspid valve on the right side of the heart.
- Saying that the P wave shows ventricular contraction.
- Giving cardiac output without units, or confusing stroke volume with cardiac output.
- Using "heart failure", "heart attack" and "cardiac arrest" as if they meant the same.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a term, a location, a count, a give-a-reason, a donor or recipient group.
- 2–3-mark questions: plasma proteins, clotting steps, donors and recipients, erythroblastosis foetalis, lymph against blood, the phases of the cardiac cycle, artery against vein, an ECG wave, a disorder.
- 5-mark questions in parts: a labelled diagram of the human heart with the flow of blood; the cardiac cycle with cardiac output; the ABO and Rh systems; regulation of the heartbeat and the ECG; disorders of circulation.

questions.stem_md: An adult has 5 litres of blood with 5 million red blood cells in every mm³. (1 litre = 10⁶ mm³.) How many red blood cells, in trillions (10¹²), does the blood contain?
questions.solution_md: Number $= 5000000 \times 5 \times 10^6 = 2.5 \times 10^{13}$; in trillions this is $2.5 \times 10^{13}/10^{12} = 25$.

questions.stem_md: A laboratory report gives a total white cell count of 12500 per mm³, of which 71 percent are neutrophils. How many neutrophils are there per mm³?
A donor gives 300 mL of whole blood. Taking plasma to be 55 percent of blood, calculate the volume of plasma in mL.

**Assertion (A):** Serum does not clot when it is left standing in a test tube.

**Reason (R):** Serum lacks fibrinogen and the other clotting factors.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true: the clotting factors were used up when the blood clotted, so serum cannot form a second clot — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Name the three main plasma proteins and state one function of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Albumin** maintains the **osmotic balance** between blood and tissues; **globulins** include the **antibodies** and so defend the body; **fibrinogen** takes part in **blood clotting**, being changed to fibrin.

questions.solution_md: Three proteins with functions.

questions.stem_md: Name the three kinds of blood corpuscle and state one structural feature and one function of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Erythrocytes (RBC):** biconcave and without a nucleus in mammals, with haemoglobin; they **carry oxygen**. **Leucocytes (WBC):** colourless and nucleated, in granulocyte and agranulocyte types; they **defend** the body by phagocytosis and antibodies. **Platelets:** small **cell fragments** from megakaryocytes; they **start blood clotting**.

questions.solution_md: Three corpuscles with features and functions.

questions.stem_md: Outline the cascade of events by which blood clots at a wound, naming the substances released and the part played by calcium ions.

answer.model_answer_md: Damaged tissue and **platelets** release **thromboplastin** (clotting factors). With **calcium ions**, it converts the inactive **prothrombin** of the plasma into **thrombin**. **Thrombin** changes soluble **fibrinogen** into insoluble **fibrin threads**, and the fibrin **meshwork traps blood cells** to form the clot.

questions.solution_md: Thromboplastin; prothrombin to thrombin with calcium; fibrinogen to fibrin.

marking_scheme.step: Thromboplastin released by platelets and tissue
Prothrombin to thrombin with calcium ions
Fibrinogen to fibrin and the clot

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the plasma protein and the enzyme that are directly involved in the formation of a blood clot. [2]
(b) A boy with a cut finger bleeds for much longer than usual, and tests show that his blood has too few platelets. Explain why this delays clotting. [2]
(c) Why is blood collected for storage in a blood bank mixed with a substance that removes calcium ions? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The plasma protein is **fibrinogen**, which is changed to insoluble fibrin, and the enzyme is **thrombin**, which brings about that change.

(b) Platelets, together with the damaged tissue, **release thromboplastin**, which starts the cascade. With **fewer platelets** less thromboplastin is released, so **thrombin and fibrin form slowly** and the clot is delayed.

(c) **Calcium ions are needed** to convert prothrombin to thrombin; if they are removed, the stored blood **does not clot**.

questions.solution_md: Fibrinogen and thrombin; role of platelets; role of calcium.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Calcium needed for thrombin, so no clotting

questions.stem_md: A patient of blood group B, Rh negative needs red cells in an emergency. Four donors are available: donor 1 is A positive, donor 2 is B positive, donor 3 is O negative and donor 4 is B negative. Which donors are safe?
questions.solution_md: The donor must have no antigen A and no Rh antigen: O negative and B negative are safe — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Four women have just delivered babies. Which one should be given an injection of anti-Rh antibodies?

options.text_md: An Rh-negative woman whose baby is Rh positive
An Rh-positive woman whose baby is Rh negative
An Rh-positive woman whose baby is Rh positive
An Rh-negative woman whose baby is Rh negative

questions.solution_md: Only when an Rh-negative mother has an Rh-positive baby can she be sensitised by its red cells — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Who discovered the ABO system of blood groups in 1900?
questions.solution_md: Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO groups; with Wiener he later reported the Rh factor — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A drop of a patient’s blood is mixed with anti-A serum, anti-B serum and anti-Rh serum on a slide. Clumping appears with the anti-A and the anti-Rh sera, but not with the anti-B serum. What is the patient’s blood group?
questions.solution_md: Clumping with anti-A shows antigen A, none with anti-B shows no antigen B, and clumping with anti-Rh shows Rh positive: A positive — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Two parents of blood group B have a child of group O. What are the genotypes of the two parents?

options.text_md: One is IᴮIᴮ and the other is Iᴮi
One is IᴬIᴮ and the other is ii

questions.solution_md: A group O child (ii) must receive i from each parent, so both group B parents are heterozygous, Iᴮi — option (b).

questions.stem_md: An Rh-positive father of genotype Dd and an Rh-negative mother (dd) are expecting a child. What is the probability that the child will be Rh positive? Give a decimal.
questions.solution_md: $Dd \times dd$ gives $Dd$ and $dd$ in equal numbers, so the probability is 0.5.

questions.stem_md: Consider the eight blood types O−, O+, A−, A+, B−, B+, AB− and AB+. For red cells, a donor type can be given to a recipient type only if the donor has no A, B or Rh antigen that the recipient lacks. Among the 64 possible donor-recipient pairs (including each type with itself), how many are compatible?
questions.solution_md: Counting the recipients of each donor: O−: 8, O+: 4, A−: 4, A+: 2, B−: 4, B+: 2, AB−: 2, AB+: 1; total = 27.

questions.stem_md: The Rh antigen was first observed in the ______ monkey.
questions.solution_md: Rhesus.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Erythroblastosis foetalis usually occurs in the first pregnancy of an Rh-negative mother who carries an Rh-positive foetus.
questions.solution_md: False. The mother makes anti-Rh antibodies mainly at the first delivery, so the risk is to a later Rh-positive foetus.

questions.stem_md: Match each ABO blood group in column I with the antibodies present in its plasma in column II.
questions.solution_md: A has anti-B, B has anti-A, AB has neither and O has both.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A person of group AB is called a universal recipient for red cells.

**Reason (R):** The plasma of a group AB person contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true, but R is false: group AB plasma has neither anti-A nor anti-B, so it cannot react with any ABO red cells — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: An Rh-negative mother is given anti-Rh antibodies soon after delivering her first Rh-positive baby.

answer.model_answer_md: The antibodies **destroy any Rh-positive foetal red cells** in her blood before she can make her own anti-Rh antibodies, which would harm a later Rh-positive baby.

questions.solution_md: Prevents sensitisation.

marking_scheme.step: They remove foetal red cells so that she does not become sensitised

questions.stem_md: What is agglutination? State how it is used to find the ABO group of a blood sample.

answer.model_answer_md: **Agglutination** is the **clumping of red cells** when an antibody meets the matching antigen. A drop of blood is mixed separately with **anti-A and anti-B sera**; **clumping with anti-A means group A**, with anti-B means group B, with both means group AB and with neither means group O.

questions.solution_md: Definition; use of sera.

marking_scheme.step: Clumping of red cells by antibody and antigen
Anti-A and anti-B sera used to interpret the result

questions.stem_md: A patient is of blood group AB, Rh negative. List all the types from which she can safely receive red cells, and explain why donors of types A positive, B positive and AB positive must be excluded.

answer.model_answer_md: She can receive red cells from **O negative, A negative, B negative, AB negative** (4 types). Her cells have antigens A and B, so she has **no anti-A or anti-B**, and all ABO groups are safe. But she is **Rh negative**, so she will make **anti-Rh antibodies** against the **Rh antigen** of A positive, B positive and AB positive donors; these must be excluded.

questions.solution_md: Four donor types; Rh reason.

marking_scheme.step: No ABO problem because she has no ABO antibodies
Rh-positive donors excluded because she is Rh negative

questions.stem_md: A Rh-negative woman is married to a Rh-positive man whose genotype is Dd. (i) What is the probability that their child will be Rh positive? (ii) In which pregnancy is an Rh-positive child at risk? (iii) What treatment is given to the mother to prevent the risk?

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The woman is dd; Dd × dd gives Dd and dd equally, so the probability of an **Rh-positive child is 0.5** (one half). (ii) The first Rh-positive child is usually safe, because the mother makes antibodies mainly after delivery, so the **second (or a later) Rh-positive child** is at risk of **erythroblastosis foetalis**. (iii) She is given **anti-Rh antibodies** soon after the first delivery.

questions.solution_md: One half; later pregnancy; anti-Rh antibodies.

marking_scheme.step: Later pregnancy at risk, with reason
Anti-Rh antibodies after the first delivery

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is the Rh factor, and name the animal in which it was first found. [1]
(b) Explain, with the sequence of events, how erythroblastosis foetalis can affect the second Rh-positive child of an Rh-negative mother. [3]
(c) How can this be prevented? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The Rh factor is an **antigen present on the surface of red cells** of Rh-positive people; it was first found in the **rhesus monkey**.

(b) During the **first delivery**, some **Rh-positive foetal red cells enter the mother’s blood**, and she makes **anti-Rh antibodies**. The first child is usually unharmed. In a **later pregnancy** with an Rh-positive foetus, these antibodies **cross the placenta** and **destroy the foetal red cells**, causing anaemia and jaundice, and sometimes death of the child.

(c) The mother is given **anti-Rh antibodies** soon after the first delivery.

questions.solution_md: Rh factor; sequence; prevention.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Antigen on red cells; rhesus monkey
(b) Foetal cells enter mother and she makes antibodies
(b) Antibodies cross the placenta in a later pregnancy
(c) Anti-Rh antibodies after the first delivery

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A hospital tested three patients with anti-A, anti-B and anti-Rh sera. A plus sign means that clumping occurred.

| Patient | anti-A | anti-B | anti-Rh |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | + | − | + |
| Q | − | − | − |
| R | + | + | − |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) O negative

**(b)** (a) P, Q and R, because Q’s red cells carry none of the three antigens

**(c)** (i) R is **AB negative**, so R’s red cells carry **antigen B**. Patient P is **A positive** and has **anti-B antibodies** in the plasma, which would **agglutinate** R’s red cells.

**OR** (ii) **Patient Q** (O negative) could safely give red cells to P, because Q’s red cells carry **no A, B or Rh antigen** for P’s antibodies to attack. Patient R could not, because R’s cells carry antigen B, against which P has anti-B.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** No clumping with any serum means that Q has no A, B or Rh antigen: O negative — option (c).

**(b)** Q is O negative, so its red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigen and can be given to all — option (a).

**(c)** (i) Antigen B meets anti-B.

(ii) Q; no antigens.

children.stem_md: What is the blood group of patient Q?
children.solution_md: No clumping with any serum means that Q has no A, B or Rh antigen: O negative — option (c).

children.stem_md: Which of the patients could safely receive red cells from Q?

options.text_md: P, Q and R, because Q’s red cells carry none of the three antigens
Only P, because P is Rh positive
Only R, because R has both A and B
Only Q, because blood groups must always match exactly

children.solution_md: Q is O negative, so its red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigen and can be given to all — option (a).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Explain why red cells from patient R must not be given to patient P.

answer.model_answer_md: R is **AB negative**, so R’s red cells carry **antigen B**. Patient P is **A positive** and has **anti-B antibodies** in the plasma, which would **agglutinate** R’s red cells.

marking_scheme.step: R’s cells carry antigen B; P has anti-B

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Which of the other two patients, Q or R, could safely give red cells to patient P? Give the reason.

answer.model_answer_md: **Patient Q** (O negative) could safely give red cells to P, because Q’s red cells carry **no A, B or Rh antigen** for P’s antibodies to attack. Patient R could not, because R’s cells carry antigen B, against which P has anti-B.

marking_scheme.step: Q’s cells have no antigens; R’s carry B

questions.stem_md: After an operation in which many lymph nodes were removed from a woman’s armpit, her arm becomes swollen. The most likely reason is that

options.text_md: too many red blood cells enter the arm
the arm is making too much lymph from platelets
the veins of the arm have lost their valves
tissue fluid that would normally return by lymph vessels collects in the arm

questions.solution_md: Lymph vessels return tissue fluid to the blood; when their drainage is blocked, fluid accumulates — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which one of these animals has an open circulatory system, with blood flowing in open spaces around the organs?
questions.solution_md: Arthropods such as the cockroach have an open circulation; annelids and vertebrates have a closed one — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Lymph flows in both directions in the lymph vessels.
questions.solution_md: False. Lymph vessels have valves, so lymph flows in one direction only, towards the veins near the heart.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: An open circulatory system supplies oxygen less quickly than a closed one.

answer.model_answer_md: In an open system blood flows in **large open spaces at low pressure**, so it moves slowly and cannot be directed.

questions.solution_md: Low pressure, slow flow.

marking_scheme.step: Low pressure and slow flow in open spaces

questions.stem_md: State two functions of lymph nodes.

answer.model_answer_md: Lymph nodes **filter the lymph**, trapping and destroying germs with the **phagocytes** in them; they also **produce and store lymphocytes**, which make antibodies and so help in defence.

questions.solution_md: Filtering; lymphocytes.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an open and a closed circulatory system, giving one example of an animal with each.

answer.model_answer_md: In an **open system** the heart pumps blood into **open spaces (sinuses)** that bathe the tissues, as in the **cockroach**; in a **closed system** the blood stays **inside vessels**, as in the **earthworm** or a mammal, which allows faster flow and better control.

questions.solution_md: Difference with two examples.

questions.stem_md: Give three differences between blood and lymph.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Red blood cells** are present in blood but **absent from lymph**.
2. Blood has **more proteins and nutrients** than lymph, which has less.
3. The white cells of lymph are mainly **lymphocytes**, while blood has all kinds of white cells and **platelets**; blood is **red**, lymph is **colourless**.

questions.solution_md: Three differences.

questions.solution_md: The left ventricle, which pumps blood to the whole body, has the thickest wall; it is marked A — option (b).

options.text_md: The left ventricle, because it receives more blood

questions.solution_md: The left auricle must push blood through a narrowed opening, so its wall works harder — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A cardiologist records the volume of blood in the left ventricle during one cardiac cycle. At the moment when the volume is falling fastest, what are the valves doing?

options.text_md: The bicuspid valve is open and the semilunar valve of the aorta is closed
The bicuspid valve is closed and the semilunar valve of the aorta is open

questions.solution_md: The volume falls as the ventricle ejects blood, with the bicuspid valve closed and the aortic semilunar valve open — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A trained swimmer has a resting heart rate of 48 beats a minute and an untrained student 72, yet at rest their cardiac outputs are the same, 5760 mL a minute. What is the best explanation?

options.text_md: The swimmer has fewer red blood cells
The swimmer’s stroke volume is larger
The swimmer’s blood pressure must be lower

questions.solution_md: Output $=$ rate $\times$ stroke volume: $48 \times 120 = 5760$, the same as $72 \times 80$, so the slower heart pumps more blood per beat — option (c).

questions.stem_md: At rest a man’s heart beats 70 times a minute and the stroke volume is 75 mL. What is his cardiac output in mL per minute?
questions.solution_md: Cardiac output $=$ stroke volume $\times$ heart rate $= 75 \times 70 = 5250$ mL per minute.

questions.stem_md: A woman’s cardiac output is 4800 mL per minute and her heart rate is 80 beats per minute. Calculate her stroke volume in mL.
questions.solution_md: Stroke volume $=$ output $/$ rate $= 4800/80 = 60$ mL.

questions.stem_md: During exercise a student’s heart beats 100 times a minute. If atrial systole stays 0.1 s and ventricular systole 0.3 s, how long, in seconds, is the joint diastole in each cycle?
questions.solution_md: Cycle $= 60/100 = 0.6$ s; joint diastole $= 0.6 - 0.4 = 0.2$ s.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The right ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta.
questions.solution_md: False. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle pumps blood into the aorta.

questions.stem_md: The thick muscular wall that separates the right and left ventricles is called the ______ septum.
questions.solution_md: Interventricular.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: The walls of the auricles are much thinner than the walls of the ventricles.

answer.model_answer_md: The auricles only **push blood a short distance into the ventricles**, whereas the ventricles must pump blood **out of the heart** to the lungs or the body.

questions.solution_md: Auricles pump a short distance.

marking_scheme.step: Auricles push blood only into the ventricles; ventricles pump it out

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: The flaps of the tricuspid valve do not turn back into the right auricle when the right ventricle contracts.

answer.model_answer_md: The flaps are held by the **chordae tendineae**, tendon-like cords attached to the **papillary muscles** of the ventricle wall.

questions.solution_md: Chordae tendineae.

questions.stem_md: Name the valve between the right auricle and the right ventricle and the valve between the left auricle and the left ventricle, and state the common function of all the valves of the heart.

answer.model_answer_md: The valve on the right is the **tricuspid valve** and on the left the **bicuspid (mitral) valve**. All the valves **allow blood to flow in one direction only** and prevent it from flowing back.

questions.solution_md: Tricuspid and bicuspid; one-way flow.

questions.stem_md: Define stroke volume and cardiac output, and state how the two are related.

answer.model_answer_md: **Stroke volume** is the **volume of blood pumped by each ventricle in one beat**; **cardiac output** is the **volume pumped by each ventricle in one minute**. **Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.**

questions.solution_md: Two definitions; relation.

marking_scheme.step: Cardiac output defined with the relation

questions.stem_md: Describe what happens in the heart during atrial systole and during ventricular systole, stating the position of the valves.

answer.model_answer_md: In **atrial systole** the **auricles contract** and push the remaining blood into the ventricles; the **valves between auricle and ventricle are open** and the semilunar valves are closed. In **ventricular systole** the **ventricles contract**, the **valves between auricle and ventricle close** and the **semilunar valves open**, so blood flows into the **pulmonary artery and the aorta**.

questions.solution_md: Atrial systole; ventricular systole with valves.

marking_scheme.step: Atrial systole: auricles contract, blood to ventricles
Ventricular systole: ventricles contract, AV valves close
Semilunar valves open and blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery

questions.stem_md: A healthy man has a heart rate of 72 per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL. A patient with heart failure has a rate of 96 per minute and a stroke volume of 40 mL. Calculate the cardiac output of each, and say by what percentage the patient’s output is lower.

answer.model_answer_md: Healthy man: $70 \times 72 = 5040$ mL per minute. Patient: $40 \times 96 = 3840$ mL per minute. The patient’s output is lower by $(5040 - 3840)/5040 \times 100 \approx 23.8$ percent, although the heart beats faster, because each beat pumps far less blood.

questions.solution_md: Two outputs; percentage fall.

(a) **Atrial (auricular) systole**, 0.1 s; **ventricular systole**, 0.3 s; **joint diastole**, 0.4 s; together the cycle lasts **0.8 s**.

(b) Cycle $= 60/100 = 0.6$ s; joint diastole $= 0.6 - 0.4 = 0.2$ s. The resting phase is **halved**, so the heart has **less time to fill** between beats while the contraction times stay the same.

**(c)** (i) Swimmer: $150 \times 170 = 25500$ mL; student: $95 \times 170 = 16150$ mL. The swimmer pumps $25500 - 16150 = 9350$ mL more a minute, because her **stroke volume is larger**, since training strengthens the heart muscle.

**OR** (ii) Her heart **pumps more blood in each beat** (a larger stroke volume), so a slower rate gives the same output. The slow rate means the heart has a **longer diastole** to fill and rest, so the heart is less strained.

**(b)** Output $=$ rate $\times$ stroke volume: swimmer $170 \times 150 = 25500$ mL, student $170 \times 95 = 16150$ mL — option (b).

**(c)** (i) Difference in output; larger stroke volume.

(ii) Larger stroke volume; longer rest.

questions.stem_md: A drug blocks the effect of the vagus nerve on the heart. What is the expected effect on the heart rate?

options.text_md: The rate falls, because the vagus nerve normally speeds the heart
The rate rises, because the slowing influence of the parasympathetic nerve is removed
The rate stops, because the SA node needs the vagus nerve to start each beat
The rate is unchanged, because the heart is not under nervous control at all

questions.solution_md: The vagus nerve (parasympathetic) slows the heart; blocking it allows the rate to rise — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student measures three blood vessels from a rabbit: vessel P has a wall 1.0 mm thick and a narrow lumen; vessel Q has a wall 0.3 mm thick, a wide lumen and flaps inside; vessel R has a wall one cell thick. Which of these is a vein?
questions.solution_md: A thin wall, a wide lumen and valve flaps identify a vein; P is an artery and R a capillary — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A drop of blood has just left the right ventricle. Through which vessel does it return to the heart, and into which chamber does it enter?

options.text_md: Pulmonary vein, into the right auricle
Vena cava, into the left auricle
Pulmonary vein, into the left auricle

questions.solution_md: From the right ventricle blood goes to the lungs and returns by the pulmonary veins to the left auricle — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A sphygmomanometer reading of a patient is 148 over 92 mm Hg. Find the difference between the systolic and the diastolic pressure (the pulse pressure) in mm Hg.
On an ECG strip that runs at 25 mm per second, the distance between two successive R peaks is 24 mm. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute, to one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: Time between beats $= 24/25 = 0.96$ s; rate $= 60/0.96 = 62.5$ beats per minute.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The arteries of the body contain valves that prevent blood from flowing backwards.
questions.solution_md: False. Valves are present in veins; arteries have thick elastic walls and carry blood under high pressure.

questions.stem_md: The impulse of the heartbeat passes from the atrio-ventricular node into the atrio-ventricular bundle, also called the bundle of ______.
questions.solution_md: His.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: The walls of arteries are elastic as well as muscular.

answer.model_answer_md: Arteries receive blood from the heart at **high pressure**, and the **elastic wall stretches and then recoils**, which withstands the pressure and keeps blood flowing.

questions.solution_md: Stretch and recoil at high pressure.

marking_scheme.step: Withstand high pressure by stretching and recoiling

questions.stem_md: What does an electrocardiogram record? State what the P wave and the T wave represent.

answer.model_answer_md: An **ECG** records the **electrical activity of the heart**. The **P wave** represents the **excitation (depolarisation) of the auricles**, and the **T wave** represents the **return of the ventricles to the normal (resting) state**.

questions.solution_md: Electrical activity; P; T.

marking_scheme.step: Records electrical activity of the heart

questions.stem_md: How do the sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves affect the heartbeat? Name one hormone that also affects it.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sympathetic** nerves **increase the heart rate and the force of the beat**, and **parasympathetic (vagus)** nerves **decrease** them. The hormone **adrenaline** (from the adrenal medulla) increases the heart rate and the cardiac output.

questions.solution_md: Sympathetic increases; parasympathetic decreases; adrenaline.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of a capillary wall and explain how it suits the function of a capillary.

answer.model_answer_md: The wall of a capillary is a **single layer of flat endothelial cells**. Because it is **only one cell thick**, oxygen, nutrients and carbon dioxide can **pass quickly by diffusion** between the blood and the tissues.

questions.solution_md: One-cell wall; rapid exchange.

marking_scheme.step: Wall of a single layer of endothelium
Thin wall allows exchange of materials

questions.stem_md: Give three structural differences between an artery and a vein, and state the direction in which each carries blood.

answer.model_answer_md: An **artery** has a **thick, elastic and muscular wall**, a **narrow lumen** and **no valves**, and carries blood **away from the heart**. A **vein** has a **thinner wall with less muscle**, a **wide lumen** and **valves**, and carries blood **towards the heart**.

questions.solution_md: Three differences; directions.

(c) Time between beats $= 24/25 = 0.96$ s; heart rate $= 60/0.96 = 62.5$ beats per minute.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly distinguishes angina pectoris from heart failure?

options.text_md: Angina is chest pain from too little oxygen reaching the heart muscle, while heart failure is the failure of the heart to pump enough blood
Angina is the failure of the heart to pump enough blood, while heart failure is chest pain
Both are other names for the stopping of the heartbeat
Angina is high blood pressure, while heart failure is low blood pressure

questions.solution_md: Angina is a pain caused by a shortage of oxygen in the heart muscle; heart failure is weak pumping — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In coronary artery disease the lumen of the coronary arteries is narrowed by deposits of

options.text_md: calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue

questions.solution_md: Atherosclerosis is the deposit of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue in the artery wall — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A patient’s blood pressure is 160 over 100 mm Hg at three separate visits. Which organs are most at risk if the condition is left untreated?

options.text_md: The heart, the brain and the kidneys
The lungs and the stomach only

questions.solution_md: Persistent hypertension damages the heart, the brain and the kidneys — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A man’s heart still beats, but it cannot pump enough blood for his body. He is breathless and fluid collects in his lungs. This condition is
questions.solution_md: A heart that beats but does not pump blood effectively enough, with congestion of the lungs, is in heart failure — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The coronary arteries supply blood to the muscle of the heart itself.
questions.solution_md: True. The coronary arteries branch from the aorta and nourish the heart muscle.

questions.stem_md: A blood pressure that is repeatedly found to be ______ over 90 mm Hg or higher is called hypertension.
questions.solution_md: 140 over 90 mm Hg.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Angina pectoris is another name for cardiac arrest.

**Reason (R):** In angina pectoris the heart suddenly stops beating.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false: angina is chest pain from too little oxygen reaching the heart muscle, and the heart goes on beating — option (d).

questions.stem_md: What causes coronary artery disease, and how does it affect the heart?

answer.model_answer_md: It is caused by the **deposition of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue** (atherosclerosis) in the **coronary arteries**, which **narrows their lumen**. Less blood and oxygen reach the **heart muscle**, which can lead to chest pain (angina) or damage.

questions.solution_md: Deposits narrow coronary arteries; less oxygen to the heart muscle.

marking_scheme.step: Less oxygen to the heart muscle

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between angina pectoris and heart failure with reference to the cause, the main symptom and the effect on the heart.

answer.model_answer_md: **Angina pectoris** is caused by **insufficient oxygen reaching the heart muscle**, often because of narrowed coronary arteries; the main symptom is **acute chest pain**, and the heart continues to pump. **Heart failure** is caused by the **heart being unable to pump blood effectively enough** for the body’s needs; the symptoms include **breathlessness and congestion of the lungs**, and the heart’s output falls.

questions.solution_md: Cause, symptom and effect for each.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is hypertension? State its cause in terms of blood pressure and two organs it can damage. [2]
(b) Explain how coronary artery disease can lead to angina pectoris. [2]
(c) How does heart failure differ from cardiac arrest? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Hypertension** is high blood pressure, **140/90 mm Hg or above** on repeated readings. It makes the heart work harder and can damage the **heart, brain and kidneys**.

(b) In **coronary artery disease** the arteries that supply the heart muscle are **narrowed by deposits** of calcium, fat and cholesterol. When the heart works harder, the **muscle does not get enough oxygen**, producing the **chest pain of angina**.

(c) In **heart failure** the heart still beats but **cannot pump blood effectively enough**; in **cardiac arrest** the heart **stops beating**.

questions.solution_md: Hypertension; CAD and angina; heart failure and cardiac arrest.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Too little oxygen on effort causes pain
